background.definition: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is rapid (hours to days) decline in renal function characterized by reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR); retention of nitrogenous waste products; and abnormalities in fluid volume, electrolytes, and acid–base homeostasis. The term AKI is now used, instead of acute renal failure (ARF), to describe a spectrum of acute changes in renal function ranging from mild alteration to renal failure requiring renal replacement therapy.AKI is a clinical diagnosis that requires interpretation of changes in kidney function in the context of the patient’s clinical picture. Although GFR can be accurately measured in research settings, changes in kidney function are usually assessed by monitoring serum creatinine and urine volume over time. Changes in serum creatinine, however, lack sensitivity for AKI because healthy people can lose nearly 50% of GFR before a change in serum creatinine is detectable. In addition, overall volume status greatly affects serum creatinine and does not necessarily reflect kidney injury.

list.listitem: Based on data from the 2001 National Hospital Discharge Survey, the frequency of acute renal failure was 19.2 per 1000 hospitalizations.

In a study of hospitalized patients between 1988 and 2002, the incidence of ARF increased from 61 to 288 per 100,000 population, the incidence of ARF requiring dialysis increased from 4 to 27 per 100,000 population, and the hospital mortality rates fell from 40.4% to 20.3%.

AKI occurs in both hospital and community settings. In database study in Scotland of 50,835 patients enrolled in 2003, 58.5% of whom had a recorded GFR of <60 mL/min/1.73m2, 4550 (8.95%) developed AKI. While most (61.1%) were hospital acquired, 22.9% were community-acquired and hospitalized within 7 days and 16.0% were community-acquired and not hospitalized.

Among patients with COVID-19, the pooled incidence of AKI was 12.3% (95% CI 9.5%-15.6%) based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 51 studies including 21,531 patients. In another scoping review and meta-analysis, the overall prevalence of AKI was estimated to be 8%. Risk factors for AKI in patients with COVID-19 include age ≥60 years (OR 3.53, 95% CI 2.92-4.25) and severe COVID-19 (OR 6.07, 95% CI 2.53-14.58).

Following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in one study, 9.1% of patients developed AKI with 4.2% requiring dialysis. A similar percentage of cases of AKI (9.8%) was reported among over 1 million patients undergoing major cardiac procedures in the United States from 2008 to 2011.
Among patients undergoing hip fracture surgery, the pooled prevalence of AKI was 17% (95% CI 14-21%) based on a meta-analysis of 11 studies with 16,421 patients.

The highest rates of AKI have been reported following in-hospital cardiac arrest. In a secondary data-analysis of the Therapeutic Hypothermia after Pediatric Cardiac Arrest In-Hospital trial conducted at 37 hospitals, 80% (249) developed AKI and 66% (207) developed severe AKI.

Although use of contrast media is associated with AKI, authors of a systematic review of 13 nonrandomized studies found similar rates of AKI, dialysis, and death among patients who underwent imaging with intravenous contrast medium compared with patients who underwent an imaging examination without contrast medium. However, authors of a meta-analysis of 45 studies with 2,830,338 patients found an average incidence of contrast-induced AKI of 6.48%.
Based on 6 retrospective cohort studies, use of IV contrast medium in patients with chronic kidney disease did not increase AKI risk (defined as deterioration in renal function).
Authors of a meta-analysis of 28 studies involving 107,335 patients found no differences in development of AKI comparing use of noncontrast vs. contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT).

Among patients undergoing coronary angiography, however, authors of a meta-analysis of 134 papers found a pooled incidence of contrast-associated AKI of 12.8% (95% CI 11.7-13.9%) with an associated mortality of 20.2% (95% CI 10.7-29.7%).

In a case series of 170 patients receiving either intra-arterial or intravenous contrast media, the risk of contrast-induced AKI (14.0% [95% CI, 9.6-20.2] vs. 11.7% [95% CI, 7.7-17.5], respectively) was similar as was mortality risk (hazard ratio 1.6 vs. 1.7, respectively) and duration of hospitalization (15 days vs. 15.5 days).

In a prospective study of contrast-induced AKI in 660 patients with GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2, the incidence was lowest following CT (0%-10.9%) and highest following noncoronary angiography (1.9%-34%); eleven patients died and 1 required dialysis.

list.listitem: Depending on the definition, ARF has been reported in 1% to 25% of ICU patients.
Among 8200 burn patients admitted to the ICU, AKI occurred in 38% (95%CI 30-46%).

Based on 33,375 patients with sepsis admitted to the ICU over 5 years in New Zealand, 42.1% had sepsis-associated AKI. Using the same database, 18.1% of patients admitted for trauma to the ICU had AKI.

Among 103 children with respiratory failure in the ICU for more than 4 days, 58% had ARF according to the RIFLE scoring system (), these patients had five times higher mortality rates than patients without ARF (25% vs. 5%).

In one retrospective 2-year study (1999-2000) of over 2000 patients hospitalized with uncomplicated ARF, median direct costs were $2600, median hospital length of stay was 5 days, and mortality was 8%.
Follow-up of this same population demonstrated the need for prolonged care in almost half; 27% required extended facility care and 22% received home health care.

In the study cited above of patients following major cardiac surgery, the mean total index hospitalization cost was $77,178 for patients with AKI compared to $38,820 for those without AKI; this represents an overall incremental annual index hospitalization AKI-associated cost of $1.01 billion.
About 75% of patients with AKI have either prerenal azotemia or acute tubular necrosis (intrinsic).

Nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., antibiotics, anti-hypertensives, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) can cause AKI. In a cohort study of ICU survivors in Scotland, 12,838 of 23,116 patients (55.5%) were given at least one community prescription of at least one nephrotoxin, 15.7% had AKI, and 5.8% received renal replacement therapy (RRT). Increased risk of RRT were associated with prescribed angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin-receptor blockers (adjusted OR 1.65, 95%CI 1.40-1.94), non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (aOR 1.12, 95%CI 1.02-1.44) and diuretics (aOR 1.35, 95%CI 1.14- 1.59).

An RCT of patients with positive blood cultures for MRSA noted no improvement in clinical outcomes (all-cause mortality, persistent bacteremia, microbiological relapse or treatment failure at 90 days) with the combination of an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam and vancomycin or daptomycin, However the group randomized to an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam experienced higher rates of AKI (23% vs 6%). In another study, concurrent use of piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin was associated with a 2 to 4-fold higher rate of AKI than monotherapy.
Several genetic loci have been identified that are associated with rapid GFR decline and may eventually help to identify individuals at high risk of deterioration of kidney function.
Causes include intravascular volume depletion from hemorrhage, GI losses, renal losses (e.g., diabetes, diuretics), and fluid sequestration (e.g., pancreatitis).
Hepatorenal syndrome can also be considered a form of prerenal AKI due to the diffuse vasoconstriction of vessels to the kidney.
SGLT-2 inhibitors cause an acute drop in GFR, but are now a pillar of prevention for AKI in high-risk groups (CKD/diabetes), despite this initial dip..

Causes include disease of large vessels (renal artery or vein thrombosis, embolism) and small vessels (e.g., vasculitis, hemolytic-uremic syndrome), acute disease of the tubulointerstitium (e.g., allergic, infectious), exogenous toxin-mediated (radiocontrast media, antibiotics) and endogenous toxin-mediated such as in rhabdomyolysis. See .

Postoperative AKI is likely due to a combination of ischemic injury and systemic inflammation. Authors of a retrospective cohort study found similar odds of AKI following surgery with and without use of general anesthesia, at 8.3% and 5.1%, respectively, although follow-up laboratory testing was less frequent among non-general anesthesia patients and prognosis, once identified, was worse.

In one review, nephrotoxic agents were implicated in up to 25% of all cases of AKI in critically-ill patients. Five cases of acute irreversible phosphate nephrotoxicity following oral sodium phosphate solution ingestion were recently reported. Authors of a meta-analysis found higher rates of AKI with use of combination vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam vs. vancomycin monotherapy (odds ratio [OR] 3.40, 95% CI 2.57-4.50) or vancomycin plus cefepime or carbapenem (OR 2.68, 95% CI 1.83-3.91).

However, when comparing cefepime with piperacillin-tazobactam for the treatment of acute infections in hospitalized patients, there was a similar occurrence of AKI, but a higher risk of coma or delirium (20.8% vs 17.3%)

Causes include ureteric obstruction (e.g., calculi, clot, cancer), bladder neck obstruction (e.g., prostatic hypertrophy, cancer), urethral obstruction (e.g., stricture), and functional disorders (e.g., neurogenic bladder).

AKI is a consequence of many different pathological conditions that sometimes lead to AKI based on the patient’s susceptibility, intensity of exposure, and presence of more than one cause. Clinical judgement is needed in addition to the above classification scheme so that a correct diagnosis can be made.

In the 2019 Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) conference, participants concluded that it may be more beneficial to distinguish between conditions that reduce glomerular function, conditions that result in injury of tubules and/or glomeruli, and conditions that do both.

Volume depletion leads to activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system with release of vasopressin and vasoconstriction of the musculocutaneous and splanchnic vascular beds. Although compensatory mechanisms (e.g., stretch receptors, vasodilator prostaglandins) preserve renal blood flow in mild hypoperfusion, these fail in severe hypoperfusion leading to a fall in GFR and ARF.

The course of illness from prerenal AKI or ischemic injury includes an initiation phase (hours to days characterized by a fall in GFR), a maintenance phase (1-2 weeks during which GFR stabilizes, urine output is at its lowest, and uremic complications are seen) and a recovery phase (characterized by increasing GFR often accompanied by marked diuresis).

Toxins and ischemic intrinsic AKI usually trigger what is classically called acute tubular necrosis, although most patients do not show this pattern of injury. The clinical picture is one of adequate renal perfusion to maintain tubular integrity but not to sustain glomerular filtration. Endothelial dysfunction, tubular cell apoptosis, coagulation abnormalities, and systemic inflammation likely play a role.
Intrarenal vasoconstriction is triggered by radiocontrast agents.

In the early stages of post-renal AKI following urinary obstruction, intraluminal pressure increases from continued glomerular filtration leading to distention within the kidney and a fall in GFR. Subsequent arteriolar vasoconstriction contributes to the reduction in GFR.

Injury-specific models may be more useful for treatment purposes because pathophysiologic mechanism may be a combination of the above categories and are often complex. These are discussed in full in the review article by Ronco et al. However, a few examples for common conditions are described here:

Renal hypoperfusion: Although hypoperfusion as noted in pre-renal AKI activates adaptive mechanisms, sustained hypoperfusion can result in organ damage (intrinsic AKI such as acute tubular necrosis). Sustained inadequate oxygen and nutrient delivery to the nephrons activates epithelial cellular injury and death which can result in renal damage and kidney dysfunction.

Nephrotoxin exposure: Toxins can act at multiple sites such as direct injury to renal tubular or endothelial cells, impaired intrarenal hemodynamics, or through precipitation of metabolites or crystals.

Sepsis: While the exact pathophysiology is unknown, mechanisms of kidney injury include macro and microvascular dysfunction, immunological and autonomic dysregulation, and abnormal cellular response to injury. Increased levels of circulating inflammatory cytokines and leucocyte activity can lead to capillary microthrombi that, along with redistribution of intrarenal perfusion, kidney inflammation, and edema, decrease capillary blood flow and oxygen delivery. Septic cardiomyopathy can contribute to renal hypoperfusion.

Adequate hydration, maintenance of adequate circulating volume (MAP), and avoidance of nephrotoxins are the cornerstones of prevention. The American Thoracic Society and others note that while adequate volume repletion is of major importance for AKI prevention, correction of fluid deficit will not always prevent renal failure. This group recommends fluid resuscitation with crystalloids; hyperoncotic solutions are not recommended because of their renal risk.
In critically ill adults, the use of balanced crystalloids (e.g., lactated Ringer’s, Plasma-Lyte) rather than 0.9% saline is associated with a lower risk of death and major adverse kidney events.

The use of hydroxyethyl starches, synthetic colloids commonly used for fluid resuscitation, increase the risk of AKI. This was confirmed in another meta-analysis in which HES products were associated with a significant increased risk of mortality and AKI after exclusion of 7 trials performed by an investigator whose research has been retracted because of scientific misconduct.

In an RCT with 389 critically-ill patients with severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.20, PaCO2 <45 mmHg, and sodium bicarbonate <20 mmol/L), there was no significant difference in 28-day all-cause death or organ failure at 7 days in those randomized to sodium bicarbonate (intervention group) vs. no sodium bicarbonate (66% in intervention group vs. 71% in control group). However, the intervention group had fewer patients requiring renal replacement therapy (35% vs. 52%). In the subgroup of patients with AKI, the intervention group fared better with fewer deaths (number needed to treat = 6), less organ failure, and increased number of vasopressor-free days.

For patients with severe CKD (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²) not on dialysis, prophylaxis consists of intravenous volume expansion with isotonic saline alone. There is no benefit to adding N-acetylcysteine (NAC) or sodium bicarbonate.

Although earlier KDIGO 2012 guidelines recommended sodium bicarbonate (with optional N-acetylcysteine) for non-dialysis patients with eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73 m² undergoing iodinated contrast studies, more recent ACR 2018 guidelines recommend prophylaxis with normal saline alone.

The updated 2018 guidelines of the European Society of Urogenital Radiology on when to administer prophylaxis against contrast-induced AKI reduced the list of risk factors to include only patients with acute or chronic renal failure, dehydration, or repeat or high-dose contrast media injection. They further recommend use of prophylaxis in patients with a GFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m2. Specific regimens are recommended in this paper.

In a RCT of 105 critically-ill ICU patients, there was no difference in rates of contrast-induced AKI using bicarbonate vs. saline (35.1% vs. 33.3%). Similarly, there was no benefit to sodium bicarbonate pre-hydration vs. no pre-hydration on contrast-induced AKI in an RCT of 523 adults with chronic kidney disease undergoing contrast-enhanced CT.
Ascorbic acid also provides protection against contrast-induced AKI, based on 9 RCTs.
Allopurinol reduced the incidence of AKI following interventional coronary procedures (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.20-0.74) based on a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs.

Statin monotherapy may be helpful in preventing contrast-induced AKI in patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD) undergoing arterial contrast medium injection. Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 8 RCTs with 2313 patients with mild to moderate renal insufficiency also found benefit of statin pretreatment, with or without N-acetylcysteine, for reducing risk of contrast induced-AKI (RR 0.59, 95%CI 0.44-0.79, I = 0%).
However, lack of benefit was demonstrated in a systematic review of 5 RCTs of rosuvastatin in patients with CKD undergoing elective cardiac catheterization.

In a systematic review, statin plus N-acetylcysteine versus N-acetylcysteine alone had benefit for reducing contrast-induced AKI (pooled RR 0.52; 0.29-0.93). In this review, there were no statistically significant benefits seen with sodium bicarbonate or ascorbic acid.

Authors of a meta-analysis found use of alprostadil, a vasodilator, helpful in reducing risk of contrast-induced AKI in patients with diabetes undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (OR 0.28; 95% CI, 0.18-0.42).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs with 2312 patients found that two tailored hydration strategies (urine flow rate-guided and central venous pressure-guided hydration) were associated with a lower incidence of contrast-induced-AKI after coronary intervention compared with fixed-rate hydration (OR 0.32, 95%CI 0.19-0.54 and OR 0.45, 95%CI 0.21-0.97, respectively).
Prostaglandin E1 reduced the incidence of contrast-induced AKI at 48 hours post-procedure (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.28-0.53) based on a meta-analysis of 7 trials.

Use of ACE inhibitors preoperatively in patients undergoing CABG may reduce the risk of AKI (6.4% vs. 12.2% in one study). In another RCT, withholding ACE inhibitors or ARBs in patients with moderate renal insufficiency undergoing cardiac catheterization did not significantly reduce the incidence of contrast-induced AKI.

IV volume expansion, both standard (average 849 ml) and intensive (average 1,574 ml) were helpful for reducing AKI in patients undergoing invasive angiography (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.49-0.77 for IV expansion versus no volume administration) based on a meta-analysis of 37 RCTs with 12,166 patients.

Use of statins in preoperative patients is controversial for reducing risk of AKI. In one study, post-operative AKI among statin initiators was 3.4% compared to 6.2% among non-initiators. Similar results were demonstrated in a meta-analysis of 15 studies of patients undergoing coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention (RR 0.63). However, in a RCT of 416 patients undergoing cardiac surgery, high-dose perioperative atorvastatin treatment compared with placebo did not reduce the risk of AKI.

Lack of benefit was also shown in a systematic review of 5 RCTs of rosuvastatin in patients with CKD undergoing elective cardiac catheterization; In another meta-analysis of high-dose perioperative atorvastatin treatment in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, authors found no difference in risk of AKI vs. placebo, and rosuvastatin increased risk of AKI in a RCT of 1922 patients scheduled for elective cardiac surgery.
Authors of a meta-analysis found significant benefit of preoperative prophylactic intraaortic balloon pump in high-risk patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting.

There are limited data to suggest that medical interventions during surgery (e.g., dopamine, diuretics, hydration fluids) can protect the kidneys of adult patients from damage. There was considerable study heterogeneity within the 72 considered studies, precluding metaanalysis.

Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO, 2012) recommends optimization of volume status and hemodynamics (using a PICCO catheter and algorithm), close monitoring of serum creatinine and urine output, avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs, discontinuation of ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers for the first 48 hours after surgery, and prevention of hyperglycemia for the first 72 hours to reduce risk of AKI in surgical patients.

Intraoperative hypotension is common, and MAP below 65 mmHg that is sustained for more than 15 minutes during surgery is associated with myocardial and renal injury. Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs with 1485 patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery found that strict blood pressure management reduced the incidence of postoperative AKI (RR 0.73, 95%CI 0.58-0.92). Maintaining intraoperative MAP above 65 mmHg in normotensive adult patients and above 70 mmHg in patients with chronic hypertension is recommended, with individualized management suggested based on other patient’s pathophysiology and clinical situations.

In an RCT of 278 undergoing cardiac surgery, use of a strategy based on KDIGO recommendations for high-risk patients (recommendations noted above; high-risk patients were identified using urinary biomarkers) compared to usual care did not reduce the number of patients developing AKI (46.3% intervention versus 41.5% control) but decreased the occurrence of moderate and severe AKI (14.0% vs 23.9%; absolute risk reduction 10.0%, 95%CI 0.9-19.1). Similarly, in an earlier RCT, patients randomized to strict use of the KDIGO recommendations had a reduced risk of both AKI (55.1% vs. 71.7%) and moderate to severe AKI compared to usual care that included keeping MAP>65 mmHg and central venous pressure between 8 and 10 mmHg.

In an RCT of 220 patients at risk of AKI following cardiac surgery, patients randomized to receive balanced forced diuresis using the RenalGuard® system (a device programed to replace urine output by infusion of a matched volume of sterile replacement solution to maintain a patient’s intravascular fluid volume) had a lower rate of post-operative AKI compared to those receiving routine care (10% vs. 20.9%, respectively).

Enhanced recovery programs for colorectal surgery, usually including restrictive intraoperative fluid management, multimodal analgesia and rapid return to diet and activity, were associated with increased risk of AKI compared to usual care (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.31-3.00) based on 6 observational studies. The authors suggested that this may be due to role of restrictive fluid administration, hemodynamic goals, and/or scheduled nephrotoxic agents in these protocols.
Neither aspirin nor clonidine administered perioperatively reduced the risk of AKI in a RCT of 6905 patients undergoing noncardiac surgery.
In a large RCT of 2932 patients undergoing CABG, off-pump vs. on-pump surgery reduced the risk of AKI (17.5% vs. 20.8%, respectively).

Remote ischemic preconditioning (RIP; 3 cycles of 5-minute ischemia and 5-minute reperfusion in one upper arm after induction of anesthesia) vs. sham preconditioning reduced the rate of AKI (37.5% vs. 52.5%) and use of RRT (5.8% vs. 15.8%) among patients undergoing elective coronary artery bypass graft. In follow-up of another positive RCT, among patients developing AKI, recovery was enhanced in patients undergoing RIP. However, in another RCT of 258 patients at high risk of death within 30 days after cardiac surgery, incidence of AKI among other outcomes was not different for RIP vs. sham conditioning.

Authors of a meta-analysis including 85 randomized comparisons found benefit of RIP on AKI (36 trials; 8493 participants; 1443 events; risk ratio 0.83, 0.71 to 0.97) based on low-quality evidence but no benefit on mortality. Reduction in incidence of AKI was confirmed in another meta-analysis of patients undergoing RIP during on-pump cardiac surgery but there was no difference in rates of RRT or on mortality.
Among patients in septic shock, use of protocol-based resuscitation did not reduce AKI compared with usual care; about 38% in each group developed AKI.

Authors of a hierarchical Bayesian network meta-analysis of 95 RCTs of medications to protect renal function after cardiac surgery concluded that atrial natriuretic peptide (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.17-0.48 based on moderate-quality evidence), B-type natriuretic peptide, dexmedetomidine, levosimendan and N-acetyl cysteine significantly decreased the rate of postoperative renal dysfunction compared with placebo. Evidence was strongest in support of atrial natriuretic peptide in patients with or without normal baseline renal function.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that "NSAIDs caused a clinically unimportant transient reduction in renal function in the early postoperative period in patients with normal preoperative renal function. NSAIDs should not be withheld from adults with normal preoperative renal function because of concerns about postoperative renal impairment."

For prevention of contrast-induced nephropathy in patients with CKD (glomerular filtration rate [GFR] <60 mL/min), choose alternate imaging not requiring contrast; if unable to do so, the single most important measure is fluid volume loading. Adults with an estimated GFR <40 mL/min are at particular risk. As noted above, however, investigators found no benefit to sodium bicarbonate pre-hydration vs. no pre-hydration on contrast-induced AKI in an RCT of 523 adults with chronic kidney disease undergoing contrast-enhanced CT.

Other at-risk patients according to National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) include those with diabetes, heart failure, renal transplant, age ≥75 years, hypovolemia, increasing volume of contrast agent, and intra-arterial administration of contrast agent.
Low-risk gadolinium-based contrast agents appear to have a large safety margin in patients with reduced renal function.

In a Cochrane review, atrial natriuretic peptide in low doses reduced the need for RRT in prevention studies (RR 0.32; 95% CI, 0.14-0.71), in patients with established AKI (RR 0.54; 95% CI, 0.30-0.98) and in prevention studies in patients after major surgery (RR 0.56; 95% CI, 0.32-0.99).
Cautious use of ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and cyclooxygenase inhibitors is strongly recommended in patients with hypovolemia or renovascular disease.

In a recent study, investigators found no benefit of using periprocedural sodium bicarbonate or acetylcysteine to prevent death or worsening kidney function in patients with CKD who are undergoing angiography. Most of the patients in the trial underwent diagnostic angiography so the volume of contrast used was small and may have resulted in lower-than-predicted event rates.

For patients on chemotherapy or at high risk of acute urate nephropathy, consider use of allopurinol (to reduce uric acid generation) and alkaline diuresis (to reduce the risk of precipitation or urate crystals in the renal tubules).

Creating systems to recognize and respond to oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h) may be helpful for patients at risk of AKI. In a before and after study of use of AKI alerts, a higher percentage of patients in the alert group received earlier therapeutic interventions (i.e., fluids, diuretics, vasopressors) than those in the pre-alert and post-alert control groups and a higher proportion of patients returned to baseline function within 8 hours.

However, investigators conducting an RCT of electronic record alerts for AKI in 6 hospitals found no differences in the primary outcome of AKI progression, receipt of dialysis, or death within 14 days of randomization between the 653 patients of 3059 with an alert compared to the 622 patients of 2971 receiving usual care (21.3% and 20.9%, respectively). Interestingly, in the two non-teaching hospitals, rates of the primary outcome were higher for the alert group (RR 1.49, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.9).

Investigate for AKI by measuring serum creatinine concentration and urine output and comparing with baseline in patients with acute illness and risk factors (as above). AKI is also diagnosed and staged based on GFR and albuminuria. C
Clinical presentation can be used to determine the cause and dominant pathophysiology of AKI, considering the categories of prerenal, intrinsic renal, or postrenal disease. C
Limited testing including UA (presence of cells, crystals, casts) and fractional excretion of sodium aid in establishing the diagnosis and its cause (). C

Additional testing that can inform diagnosis, management, and prognosis includes serial serum creatinine, potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid, creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, eosinophils, daily urine output, and the furosemide stress test. C The role of biomarkers in AKI risk stratification is under investigation.
In cases of intrinsic AKI that remain undiagnosed, renal biopsy may be needed. C

list.listitem: International consensus criteria for AKI are offered by KDIGO (2012). AKI is defined as an acute change (<=7 days) in serum creatinine of 1.5 times baseline or 0.3 mg/dL or more within a 48-hour period OR urine volume of <0.5 mL/kg over 6 or more hours. KDIGO stages of acute kidney injury are shown in . Data support a correlation between kidney injury (e.g., cell sloughing) and more severe stages of AKI.

In 2019, KDIGO held a controversies conference to identify ongoing controversies and determine best practices and areas of uncertainty in prevention and management of AKI. The group concluded that serum creatinine and urine output continue to be used to define AKI and that updated guidelines address both the role of these measurements and how best to determine baseline kidney function.

A consensus panel (acute dialysis quality initiative) developed the RIFLE criteria for AKI with three classifications of increasing severity [risk (R), injury (I), and failure (F)] and two outcome categories [loss (L) and end-stage kidney disease (E)]. The two outcome criteria are determined by the persistence of ARF—loss is complete loss of kidney function for >4 weeks and end stage is complete loss of kidney function of >3 months. See , this set of characteristics goes beyond defining ARF to describe a spectrum of acute changes in renal function ranging from mild changes to renal failure requiring RRT.
Based on the RIFLE criteria (), a serum creatinine of ≥4 mg/dL is used as a cutoff for renal failure.
Oliguria is defined as urine output <400 mL/d.
Anuria is defined as urine output <100 mL/d.

Clues to a predominantly prerenal etiology include symptoms of dizziness, thirst, dry mouth, and physical signs including tachycardia, poor skin turgor, reduced jugular venous distention, and orthostatic hypotension.

Medications should be reviewed, particular new ones, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antihypertensive agents, and nephrotoxic medications (see ), these can cause either prerenal or intrinsic renal AKI.

Clues to possible intrinsic renal AKI include recent major surgery; recent septic shock; flank pain (renal artery or vein occlusion); oliguria, edema, hypertension (acute glomerulonephritis or vasculitis); severe hypertension, papilledema, hypertensive retinopathy (malignant hypertension); fever, arthralgia, skin rash (allergic interstitial nephritis).
Renal vasculitis presents as a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis characterized by ARF, hematuria, and proteinuria.
Clues to a likely postrenal AKI include history of benign prostatic hypertrophy, suprapubic or colicky flank pain, complete anuria, and use of anticholinergic medication.

KDIGO (2012) defines AKI using serum creatinine of 1.5 times baseline or 0.3 mg/dL or more within a 48-hour period OR urine volume of <0.5 mL/kg over 6 or more hours (see ). The 2019 NICE guideline also recommends investigating for AKI by measuring serum creatinine concentration. They suggest that AKI can be diagnosed by a rise in serum creatinine of 26 micromoles/L (0.29 mg/dL) within 48 hours or a 50% or greater rise in serum creatinine compared to baseline known or presumed to have occurred in the past 7 days. Options for further identifying the cause are displayed in interactive flowcharts.

If the patient has a condition affecting serum creatinine independent of GFR (e.g., extremes of muscle mass or diet), or interference with the assay, cystatin C should be measured and estimated GFR should be calculated and reported using cystatin C and serum creatinine or GFR should be measured directly using a clearance procedure. Albuminuria can be measured using urine albumin and creatinine in an untimed spot urine collection and reporting albumin-to-creatinine ratio or with an albumin excretion rate measured from a timed urine collection.
Future guidelines are expected to assist with risk stratification including AKI duration (particularly>48 hours), location of initial diagnosis (community vs. hospital), and biomarkers.
UA in patients with prerenal AKI typically shows hyaline casts and elevated specific gravity (>1.018). NICE recommends a UA in all patients when AKI is suspected or confirmed.

UA in patients with intrinsic renal disease typically shows hematuria, proteinuria, red cell or granular casts; patients with AKI from ischemia often have muddy brown granular or tubular epithelial cell casts and specific gravity <1.015.
Urate crystals suggest gout or tumor lysis, while oxalate crystals suggest multiple myeloma.
UA in patients with bilateral pyelonephritis typically show red and white blood cells, proteinuria, and bacteriuria.
Hematuria may indicate stones, prostatic hypertrophy, or tumor.

Laboratory tests from serum that may be useful for both diagnosis and management of complications include serial measurement of serum creatinine (radiocontrast nephropathy associated with rapid rise peaking at 3-5 days; ischemia-associated AKI creatinine peaks at 7-10 days), potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid, creatine kinase (MM band suggests rhabdomyolysis), lactate dehydrogenase (increases in urate nephropathy and tumor lysis), and eosinophils (suggests allergic interstitial disease).

Fractional excretion of sodium (urine sodium times plasma creatinine divided by the product of plasma sodium times urine creatinine; the result multiplied by 100) is useful for distinguishing between prerenal and intrinsic renal causes of AKI. This test relates the sodium to creatinine clearance (sodium is avidly reabsorbed in prerenal AKI, increasing the denominator of the equation) and the result is typically <1% in prerenal AKI (LR+ 37). Exceptions include patients with bicarbonaturia, underlying chronic renal failure, and those with adrenal insufficiency. The FeNa test can still be used for patients on diuretics but the best cutoff is ≤35%.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies with 872 patients found a pooled sensitivity and specificity for differentiating intrinsic from prerenal AKI of 90% (95%CI 81% to 95%) and 82% (95%CI 70% to 90%), respectively, using a threshold of 1%; the test performed best in patients with oliguria. Both sensitivity and specificity were lower for patients with a history of CKD or using diuretics making this test of less value in those cases.

The furosemide stress test (FST) appears useful for identifying patients who are likely to have progressive disease and need RRT or dialysis; however, this test is of yet unregulated and its role in evaluation remains unclear. The test is performed by IV infusion of furosemide (1.0 or 1.5 mg/kg) and measuring urine output for 2 hours afterward. A positive test is a 2-hour urinary output of 200 ml or less.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 trials found the pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios for the FST of 0.81 (95% CI 0.74-0.87), 0.88 (95% CI 0.82-0.92), 5.45 (95% CI 3.96-7.50), and 0.26 (95% CI 0.19-0.36), respectively, for AKI progression prediction with a summary receiver operating characteristics curve for diagnostic accuracy of 0.88. Similar results were found for prediction of need for RRT with a positive and negative likelihood ratio of 3.16 (95% CI 2.06-4.86) and 0.25 (95% CI 0.14-0.44), respectively.

Biomarkers of AKI can be conceptualized based on AKI stage – from stress to damage to kidney dysfunction. Urinary tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-2 (TIMP-2) and insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 7 (IGFBP7) are indicators of kidney stress and have been seen immediately after cardiopulmonary bypass. Urinary neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), kidney injury marker 1, and liver-type fatty acid binding protein are indicators of kidney damage and serum or urine cystatin C and serum pro-enkephalin are markers of filtration and kidney dysfunction.

A combination of urine TIMP-2 and IGFBP7 in a pooled analysis of 9 studies exhibited moderate diagnostic accuracy for AKI with a summary receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.86 (95% CI 0.82-0.88). Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 studies of critically-ill patients found that using a urinary TIMP-2 and IGFBP7 cut-off of 0.3 ng/ml/1000 (high sensitivity) or 2.0 ng/ml/1000 (high specificity) could be used to accurately predict AKI with an associated area under the curve of 0.748 for the former cut-off value and 0.844 for the latter.

neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), in one study, was better at distinguishing AKI from prerenal azotemia and CKD than serum creatinine, and, in a meta-analysis, both serum or urine NGAL were similarly useful in diagnosis and prognosis (predicting RRT) of AKI, especially in children. A cutoff of 134 ng/ml for NGAL was associated with AKI among patients admitted with heart failure in one study (sensitivity 85%, specificity 80%; area under the curve 0.81).
Two other biomarkers, urinary L-type fatty acid-binding protein and N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminidase were useful in another study for predicting AKI in adult patients following heart surgery.

Other potential markers include kidney injury molecule-1, cysteine-rich protein 61, spermidine/spermine N(1)-acetyltransferase, cystatin C, urine interleukin-18, and procalcitonin. In one study, decreased levels of insulin-like growth factor and cholesterol in addition to sepsis and oliguria were associated with higher mortality in patients with AKI.

Ultrasonography is useful, particularly when postrenal AKI is suspected (will show ureteral obstruction and/or hydronephrosis). Patients with chronic kidney disease may have small kidneys with a thin cortex. The American College of Radiology recommends reserving duplex Doppler for suspected renal artery stenosis or thrombosis. If obstruction is identified, further delineation or location can be visualized using retrograde or anterograde pyelography. If the cause of obstruction remains undetermined following ultrasound, MRI or nonenhanced CT may be appropriate, particularly for urinary tract obstruction.

Ultrasound can also be considered for patients with no identified cause for AKI. The American College of Radiology (ACR) supports performing ultrasound in these cases; NICE concurs, especially if the patient is at risk of urinary tract obstruction.

Renal biopsy may be indicated for patients with intrinsic kidney disease that remains undiagnosed. ACR recommends percutaneous ultrasound-guided renal biopsy especially in patients with acute inflammatory conditions such as nephritis.
Several clinical rules are available, including a creatinine clearance calculator, a tool to interpret fractional excretion of sodium, and the MDRD 6 variable tool for estimating GFR.

In a database investigation of general surgery patients (AKI occurs in approximately 1%), patients who had 6 of 11 risk factors (age 56 years or older, male sex, emergency surgery, intraperitoneal surgery, diabetes mellitus on oral therapy or insulin, active congestive heart failure, ascites, hypertension, mild or moderate preoperative renal insufficiency) had a 9% rate of AKI.

Most prediction models for contrast-induced nephropathy have only modest ability, are primarily relevant to patients receiving contrast for coronary angiography, and have not been evaluated for their effect on clinical decision making or patient outcomes.

In a review of prediction rules for AKI requiring dialysis after cardiac surgery, the Cleveland Clinic model, including gender, prior heart surgery, preoperative renal insufficiency or intra-aortic balloon pump use, and chronic illnesses, was found to have high discrimination in most of the tested populations.

Adding preoperative urine albumin to creatinine ratio to a clinical model slightly improved prediction of AKI (area under the curve 0.70). Preoperative brain natriuretic peptide level is also associated with postoperative AKI.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient with AKI. Treating the underlying cause or trigger and avoiding further insults are key principles.
Daily monitoring of urine output and creatinine is used to determine severity and prognosis () in addition to monitoring response to treatment.
If the patient meets criteria for renal failure (), RRT is usually indicated in the presence of volume overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, overt uremia, and progressive azotemia.

Treatment is based on etiology;; a “one-size fits all” approach is discouraged and fluid administration should be guided by the clinical context and hemodynamic assessment, with repeated monitoring. For prerenal AKI, replace volume loss avoiding overhydration, and treat underlying disease (GI, hepatic, renal, pancreatic, cardiac). For intrinsic AKI, eliminate toxins and consider use of glucocorticoids and alkalinizing agents. For postrenal AKI, relieve obstruction and treat the underlying cause. C
Use of furosemide and low-dose dopamine do not appear to be effective in the treatment of AKI. A
Consider continuous administration of cyclophosphamide or plasmapheresis for patients with renal vasculitis. A

Indications for RRT include volume overload, hyperkalemia (>7 mmol/L or electrocardiographic signs of hyperkalemia), metabolic acidosis, overt uremia, and severe (urea >30–35 mmol/L or creatinine >300–400 μmol/L) or progressive azotemia. C

Early (within 12 hours of diagnosis) vs. late (48 hours after diagnosis) renal replacement therapy (RRT) is associated with equivalent outcomes in critically-ill patients with septic shock and severe AKI. B

In a meta-analysis, use of furosemide was not effective in preventing or treating ARF (to correct oliguria or anuria) in the hospital setting; nor does it reduce mortality in patients with AKI. One cohort study performed in the intensive care unit (ICU) also found no benefit to the use of diuretics in AKI.

Low-dose (renal-dose) dopamine (1-3 mcg/kg/min) did not improve outcomes in patients with or at risk for AKI based on a meta-analysis, despite some short-term improvement in measures of renal function.
Atrial natriuretic peptide may benefit patients with AKI as a treatment, in addition to its preventive effects.

Use of ACE inhibitors and ARBs in patients 6-months following hospital discharge for AKI was associated with a significantly lower risk of death (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.72-0.90) with over 1-year of follow-up based on 5 cohort studies with 153,174 patients.
Continuous administration of cyclophosphamide increases remission and results in fewer relapses in patients with renal vasculitis.

Fenoldopam infusion, an antihypertensive drug which acts as a selective D1 receptor partial agonist vs. placebo did not reduce the need for RRT or risk of 30-day mortality among patients with AKI after cardiac surgery.
For patients with acute glomerulonephritis or vasculitis, glucocorticoids, and alkalinizing agents are options.

For patients with postrenal causes, relief of obstruction can lead to resolution of AKI; bladder or percutaneous catheterization or placement of stents may be a useful interim strategy depending on the level of the obstruction.
In patients with cirrhosis, large volume paracentesis may be useful.

RRT can be performed by several techniques including intermittent hemodialysis, slow extended daily dialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and continuous RRT. There is insufficient evidence to support one method over another. In one large trial, intensive renal support in critically ill patients with AKI and failure did not improve outcomes.

Although some studies found that early initiation of RRT may be associated with a survival advantage, authors of a meta-analysis of 12 trials found no differences in an early vs. delayed strategy of RRT on mortality. A delayed strategy of RRT initiation, defined as initiation if severe hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary edema, blood urea nitrogen level higher than 112 mg per deciliter, or oliguria for more than 72 hours occurred after randomization, and may avert the need for RRT in an appreciable number of patients.

In an RCT of critically-ill patients with septic shock and severe AKI, delaying RRT for 48 hours compared to initiation within 12 hours had no influence on 90-day mortality (54% vs. 58%, respectively), number of days free from mechanical ventilator and vasopressor use or in intensive care unit or hospital length of stay. Among patients in the delayed group, almost 30% had spontaneous renal recovery and 17% underwent emergency RRT prior to 48 hours.

Similar results were reported in an RCT of 3019 critically-ill patients, showing comparable 90-day mortality rates of 43.9% in the accelerated-strategy group and 43.7% in the standard-strategy group, an RCT of 2927 critically-ill patients with severe AKI (about 44% 90-day mortality in each group), and a meta-analysis.

Another RCT of 2927 critically ill patients with acute kidney injury, half of whom recieved accelerated RRT (i.e. within 12 hours of enrollment) and half of whom recieved RRT only in the presence of hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis, severe respiratory failure, or persistent acute kidney injury for at least 72 hours demonstrated no differences in 90-day mortality rates; but more adverse events, greater risk of re-hospitalization and RRT dependency, in the accelerated RRT group. strategy group, patients started RRT within 12 hours of confirmation of full eligibility. In the standard group, RRT was only started if patients had evidence of hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis, severe respiratory failure, or persistent acute kidney injury for at least 72 hours.

A meta-analysis of 15 studies found no advantage of continuous over intermittent RRT on patient outcomes. The most recent meta-analysis of 23 studies confirmed no advantage between type of RRT (continuous, intermittent, hybrid) or peritoneal dialysis for critically-ill patients with AKI.
Authors of another metaanalysis concluded that high-dose vs. standard-dose RRT in AKI offered no advantages in patient survival or recovery of renal function.

Among critically-ill patients with AKI, there was no benefit of continuous RRT compared to sustained low efficiency dialysis with respect to mortality (rate ratio [RR] 0.67, 95%CI 0.44-1.00), renal recovery (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.83-1.42), or dialysis dependence (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.69-1.53) based on a meta-analysis of 11 studies with 1160 patients.

Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) significantly reduces the risk of end-stage renal disease in patients with renal vasculitis. However, plasmapheresis does not appear to be effective in patients with multiple myeloma-associated renal failure.

Enteral or parenteral nutritional support does not generally benefit patients with AKI. In this review, a single study reported a significant increase in recovery rate for AKI and survival in patients on dialysis with intravenous essential L-amino acids (EAA) compared to hypertonic glucose alone. Recommendations for use of EAA are limited by the small number of participants enrolled in studies and the overall poor quality of existing studies.There were no outcome differences using lower vs. higher calorie-total parenteral nutrition.
In two RCTs, the use of thyroid hormone therapy in patients with AKI is associated with worse renal outcomes than controls or comparison treatments.
At the 2019 KDIGO conference, recommendations were offered regarding involvement of nephrology-based care providers based on prolonged AKI and for patients with stage 2 or 3 AKI.

NICE recommends discussing AKI management with a nephrologist within 24 hours of detection when one or more of the following is present: a possible diagnosis that may need specialist treatment (e.g., vasculitis, glomerulonephritis), no clear cause, inadequate treatment response, associated complications, stage 3 AKI, renal transplant, or CKD stage 4 or 5 (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2).

Sustained AKI leads to disturbances in fluid, electrolyte, acid–base balance, and hormonal regulation. In addition, many patients experience abnormalities in the CNS, coagulation system, and immune system.

Conventional indications for renal replacement therapy include volume overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, overt uremia, and progressive azotemia; precise definitions of these indicators is lacking.
The RIFLE criteria () can be used to estimate mortality risk. B
Most patients recover from AKI, although elderly patients and those with severe AKI or who do not recover fully from AKI have a poorer prognosis. B
Prognosis is poor (mortality 70% in one study) for ICU patients with AKI who require dialysis. B

Using the RIFLE criteria (see Diagnostic Criteria) to classify 247 patients in the ICU with elevated serum creatinine (>150 µmol/L), mortality was greatest in patients classified as F (74.5%) compared to patients classified as I (50%) or R (38.3%).
In a larger multicenter study of over 5000 patients in the ICU, AKI was seen in 67% (12% R, 27% I, and 28% classified as F). In the 1510 patients who reached R, 56% progressed to I or F.

In a retrospective study of burn patients over a 2-year period in one institution, AKI occurred in about half of the 17 patients in the RIFLE Failure category, with an associated mortality rate of 34.4%. Maximum SOFA score, presence of sepsis, and F class of AKI were the independent risk factors for mortality.

Nearly two-thirds of AKI cases resolve within 7 days. Among patients whose AKI did not resolve by hospital discharge, hospital mortality was 47% and, among those discharged alive, 1-year survival was 77%. In contrast, prognosis is good even for those with more severe AKI (stage 2-3) who fully recover by hospital discharge; one-year survival for these patients was over 90%.
In a systematic review of studies on renal failure, investigators found decreased recovery of kidney function in patients over age 64 years compared to younger patients (69% vs. 74%).

In a follow-up cohort study of 425 survivors of severe acute kidney disease who had no preexisting kidney disease, 57% had complete recovery and 43% had partial recovery at discharge. During the first year after discharge, however, 18% of survivors died and at 5 years, only 25% of the cohort were still alive.
A systematic review of 31 studies identified urinary C-C motif chemokine ligand 14 (CCL14) as the biomarker that best predicted persistent acute kidney injury (AUC = 0.807).

Following cardiac surgery, the 1- and 2-year overall survival rates of patients with AKI were significantly lower than that for non-AKI patients (85.9% and 82.3% vs. 98.1% and 93.7%); survival was lower even after recovery of AKI. Factors associated with 2-year survival included age, CKD, diabetes, cardiopulmonary bypass time and length of ICU stay.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 17 studies confirmed poorer outcomes associated with AKI following cardiac surgery including higher mortality (OR 6.27; 95% CI, 3.58-11.00) and longer hospital length of stay (SMD = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.02-0.88).

Among patients enrolled in two RCTs, AKI following coronary artery bypass grafting for acute coronary syndrome, occurring in one third of patients, vs. no AKI was associated with higher one-month and one-year mortality (6.7% vs. 2.2% and 10.4% vs. 4.3%, respectively) and one-month and one-year major adverse cardiac events (17.6% vs. 12.4% and 22.0% vs. 15.3%, respectively).

The duration of AKI after cardiac surgery is directly proportional to long-term mortality. In one study, the adjusted hazard ratio for survival compared to those without AKI was 1.66 (1.32-2.09) for a duration of 1 to 2 days and 3.40 (2.73-4.25) for a duration of 7 or more days.

A study compared a continuous infusion of amino acids (Isopuramin 10%) at 2g per kg from the start of surgery up to 72 hours (or until discharge from the ICU, initiation of kidney replacement therapy, or death) in 1759 patients with matching placebo consisting of Ringer’s solution in 1752 patients. The continuous infusion of amino acids for patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass decreases the risk of postoperative AKI but does not affect 30-day mortality or the need for or duration of kidney replacement therapy. Of note, 98% of the study population was White, thus limiting the generalizability of these findings.

Mortality rates among patients in the ICU with AKI range from 15% to 60%, depending on the definition of ARF. Even patients with a single episode of mild AKI have significantly lower long-term survival rates than critically-ill patients with no AKI (10-year adjusted mortality hazard ratio 1.53; 95% CI, 1.2-2.0 for 28-day survivors with stage 1 AKI compared with critically-ill patients with no AKI). In a cohort study of 132 patients in the ICU with AKI who required dialysis, in-hospital mortality was 70% and 33% of survivors required continued dialysis.
Among 2,719 Finnish patients admitted to the general ICU, the absolute excess 90-day mortality attributable to AKI was 8.6% and the population attributable risk was 19.6%.

In a Canadian population-based study, there was an increased incidence rate of chronic dialysis among individuals with AKI requiring in-hospital dialysis compared with a control group (2.63 per 100 person-years vs. 0.91 per 100 person-years, respectively), but no increase in all-cause mortality rate.

In a follow-up study of 206 IUC patients with AKI requiring RRT, 95 (46%) survived at 90 days and the mortality at 3 years was 50% for those with preexisting kidney disease, and 71% and 82% for those with de novo and without CKD, respectively.
Sepsis-associated AKI was associated with higher odds of death (19.8% vs. 13.4%; OR 1.6 [1.5-1.7]). Contrast-induced nephropathy is associated with increased 30-day mortality.

In a derivation and validation study of features that predict the development of chronic kidney disease in patient presenting with AKI, a 6-variable model (older age, female sex, higher baseline serum creatinine, albuminuria, greater acute kidney injury severity, and higher discharge serum creatinine level) performed extremely well in predicting the risk of chronic kidney disease.
Urine output and creatinine levels should be followed daily; improvement with fluids or treatment of the underlying cause is an indication of injury only.
The RIFLE criteria () can be applied to help to assist in prognosis.
In acute renal failure, a stable survival rate is not achieved until after 30 to 60 days.

Post-AKI follow-up recommendations based on severity were offered by participants at the 2019 KDIGO conference and included: Stage 1, short duration, recovered: consider, at one year, KAMPS bundle (Kidney function check [serum creatinine/GFR and albuminuria, proteinuria]–Advocacy [education and care coordination]–Medications [attention to those excreted by the kidneys and nephrotoxic drugs]– [blood] Pressure–and Sick day protocol [medications to withhold/avoid/monitor]. Stage 1, no prior chronic kidney disease, increasing co-morbidities, serum creatinine not returning to baseline: consider KAMPS bundle at 6 months. Prolonged stage 1 or stage 2, serum creatinine <25% of preexisting baseline: Labs in the next 3-6 weeks with long-term KAMPS and nephrology appointment within several months. Prolonged stage 2 with urinalysis showing injury, multiple co-morbidities, serum creatinine >25% of preexisting baseline but some recovery: Labs in the next 1-2 weeks with KAMPS and nephrology appointment within one week. Stage 3 AKI and persistent or other forms of kidney disease: Labs within days of discharge and follow-up with nephrology; KAMPS within 1 week.
In older patients, there is evidence that serum creatinine underestimates renal function, while formulas used to estimate creatinine clearance based on serum creatinine overestimate renal function.
Caution should be used prior to initiating medications in the elderly.
In a systematic review of studies on renal failure, investigators found decreased recovery of kidney function in the elderly (older than 64 years) compared to younger patients (69% vs. 74%).
Among children undergoing cardiac surgery, age ≤2 years or over 13 years and longer cardiopulmonary bypass time were independently associated with AKI. The latter may be a proxy for illness severity.

Among children who suffered cardiac arrest, severe AKI, occurring in 66%, was associated with significantly decreased hospital survival (48% vs 65%) and decreased 12-month survival with favorable neurobehavioral outcome (30% vs 53%).

cell.label: Patient with suspected acute kidney injury. Clinically compatible with prerenal cause (e.g., anemia, dizziness, nausea/vomiting, orthostasis)?
Consider prerenal causes: hemorrhage, GI loss, renal loss, fluid sequestration, sepsis, and low cardiac output.
Clinically compatible with obstruction (e.g., suprapubic or flank pain, anuria)?
Perform UA and fractional sodium excretion.
Fractional sodium excretion <1% (<35% if on diuretics)?
Suspect ischemic or nephrotoxic kidney injury.
Primarily RBC: suspect stones, BPH, tumor; obtain ultrasound. RBC, WBC, proteinuria, bacteruria: consider infection.
Diagnosis still unclear? Consider renal biopsy.

RBC casts, proteinuria: suspect glomerulonephritis or vasculitis; obtain lab data. Muddy brown granular or tubular epithelial cell casts: suspect ischemia, consider angiogram. WBC, granular casts: suspect interstitial nephritis (check drugs).
Withdraw toxin; supportive treatment based on lab data.
Obtain ultrasound (see chapters on benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), renal lithiasis, urinary retention, bladder tumors).

feature.caption: Toxins That Can Cause Acute Renal Failure.
feature.feature_body:
Endogenous
● Rhabdomyolysis (e.g., trauma, seizures, acute muscle ischemia, intoxicants)
● Hemolysis (e.g., massive blood transfusion reaction)
● Hypercalcemia/hypercalcuria (e.g., malignancy, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D-related)
● Hyperuricemia/hyperuricosuria (inherited, treatment of myeloproliferative disorders)
● Hyperoxaluria (e.g., inherited, low-calcium diet, small bowel disease)
● Plasma cell dyscrasia (e.g., multiple myeloma)
Exogenous
Radiocontrast agents drugs
● Allopurinol
● ACEIs and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) (hemodynamically mediated)
● Antibioticsa
● Chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin)
● Cimetidine
● Cyclosporine
● Diuretics (e.g., bumetanide, furosemide, thiazide-type)
● 5-Aminosalicylates
● Lansoprazole and omeprazole
● Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugsb (risk may be lower with more selective agents; hemodynamically mediated)
● Quinine, quinidine
● Statins (e.g., lovastatin)
Toxic substance exposure
● Heavy metals (e.g., lead, mercury)
● Organic solvents (e.g., ethylene glycol)
● Antibiotics commonly associated with acute tubular necrosis include aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cephalosporins, tetracycline, and vancomycin; those associated with acute interstitial nephritis include ciprofloxacin, indinavir, penicillins, rifampin, and sulfonamides
